title: Just look at him (Teresa, Way of Perfection 26)
hookLine: I'm not asking you to think much, only to look at him
tomorrow: what fits on a bookmark and holds up a whole life?

cards: Ten minutes set aside to pray, and the mind is already at the group chat, the unpaid bill, the thing somebody said at lunch. Push harder for holy thoughts and they slip away faster. Teresa knew that kind of prayer time.
Writing to the sisters of her convent in The Way of Perfection, she does something kind: she lowers the bar almost to the floor.

teach.b: Here's the heart of it, in the sense of chapter twenty-six: I'm not asking you to think much about him, or come up with many ideas, or make long, clever meditations. I'm only asking you to look at him. Not analyze.
Look. And she asks: who could stop you turning the eyes of your soul toward him, even for a moment? Then she makes it personal.
Meet him where you are. If you're glad, look at him risen. If you're struggling or sad, look at him on the way to the garden, or carrying the cross.
Whatever the mood, there's a scene that fits it.
Then the part that turns it around: he is already looking at you. You aren't trying to catch his attention; you're returning a gaze.
The letter to the Hebrews comes close: "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith." Teresa's version is gentler. Not a test of concentration.
A glance, and then another, every time the mind wanders off and comes back. In her picture, the wandering isn't the failure.
It's the moment to look again.

how: Some Christians pray by simply looking at a cross or an icon in silence; in some Orthodox and Catholic homes an icon corner or a crucifix gives the eyes a place to rest.

games.q: what does “just look at him” mean?
o: prayer as a glance toward Christ, again and again
staring at a statue until you have a vision
watching other people pray to learn how

games.q: just look at him — tap the pairs.
p: look at him carrying the cross

s: a wandering mind means the prayer has failed
the likely worry. in Teresa's picture, wandering is the moment to look again.
Teresa says he is already looking at you
you're returning a gaze, not trying to catch his attention.
Teresa asks her sisters for long, clever meditations
she asks them not to think much, only to look at him.

games.q: your neighbor has three kids, a night job and a brain that never stops. she says, 'I can't focus, so I can't pray.' what would Teresa offer her?
o: a quiet retreat weekend before she tries again.
a glance toward him, and another when she drifts.
a longer list of holy things to think about.
games.why: Teresa lowers the bar: not long meditations, only a look toward him, and again when the mind wanders. he's already looking.

practice: If there's an image of Christ near you, a cross, an icon, a painting on your phone, rest your eyes on it. Don't think about it; just look, and when your mind wanders, come back to looking.
If that image isn't yours, look at one thing in front of you with the same quiet attention.

wordCard.voice: Just look at him. Teresa's prayer for wandering minds: not more thoughts, only a glance toward him.

orig.note: Teresa's Spanish verb for look, written in the Latin alphabet.

carryVoice: Keep this one: just look at him, and look again whenever the mind wanders. Day sixteen fifty.
